transcript:
Fireflies.ai transcript

Meeting title: Technical Deep Dive: Dedicated Burst Capacity (design partner)
Date: Wed, Jun 18, 2025
Start time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 56 minutes

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference)
- Mina Haddad (Redwood Inference)
- Jordan Lee (Redwood Inference)
- Logan Wright (Redwood Inference)
- Peter Holtz (Redwood Inference)
- Amit Shah (HelioPay)
- Sara Liu (HelioPay)
- Dylan Moore (HelioPay)
- Grace Kim (HelioPay)

Summary (auto-generated)
HelioPay walked through their weekly and month-end traffic spikes on Dedicated and asked how Redwood’s “burst capacity” behaves under contention. Redwood explained the v1 approach: strict admission control into region/GPU-specific burst pools (hard caps + fairness + saturation gates + cooldown) rather than preemption. The group aligned on fallback semantics (baseline → burst → optional fallback model/region → deny) and customer-visible observability (admit/deny counters, burst token attribution, latency breakdown). Open questions centered on deny response codes and retry guidance, and how residency/isolation is maintained when using shared burst pools.

Topics
- What “burst” is (and isn’t) in v1
- Admission control, fairness, and cooldowns
- Per-tenant limits (concurrency, tokens/sec, windows)
- Routing fallbacks and denial semantics (429 vs 503)
- Monitoring expectations (customer + internal dashboards)
- Security: isolation, audit logs, residency, and KMS

Action items
- Markus Klein - Send HelioPay the draft burst schema and example config + deny reason codes by 2025-06-20
- Logan Wright - Send metric names/dimensions for burst visibility and recommended alert thresholds by 2025-06-21
- Mina Haddad - Follow up with a short write-up of fallback order and what is configurable in pilot by 2025-06-20
- HelioPay (Amit Shah) - Provide traffic spike characterization and target SLOs (p99 latency and throughput goals) by 2025-06-24

Questions (captured)
- If burst pool is full, do we get a fast fail (and can we distinguish “you hit your limit” vs “pool saturated”)?
- If a request is admitted to burst, can it be preempted mid-generation?
- Will burst ever route cross-region (data residency)?
- Can we cap burst by model, or by endpoint / route?

Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, thanks everyone for joining. This is the technical deep dive on the Dedicated burst option. We’ve got Mina from routing, Jordan from policy, Logan from telemetry, Peter SRE embed. Um, we’ll keep this pretty practical.

[00:18] Amit Shah: Great. Yeah, thanks Markus. We’re excited but also… we need to understand like, the exact behavior under stress. Because we don’t want surprise noisy neighbor stuff.

[00:30] Markus Klein: Totally. Maybe quick intros and then we’ll go straight into your spike shape and then we’ll map that to admission + fallback.

[00:37] Mina Haddad: Mina, I run smart routing for Redwood Dedicated and Hosted.

[00:41] Jordan Lee: Jordan, I’m on the control plane policy engine side.

[00:45] Logan Wright: Logan, telemetry and metering.

[00:48] Peter Holtz: Peter, I’m the SRE embed for routing, on-call for the pilot rollout.

[00:53] Amit Shah: Amit, platform engineering. Sara is our SRE. Dylan is ML. Grace from security.

[01:01] Sara Liu: Hi.

[01:02] Dylan Moore: Hey.

[01:03] Grace Kim: Hi.

[01:05] Markus Klein: Cool. Amit, do you want to restate the core problem? I know from earlier calls it’s the weekly batch spikes.

[01:14] Amit Shah: Yeah. So, we have a Dedicated tenant in us-east. Baseline traffic is stable, but we have, like, every Friday we run this reconciliation job, and then month-end it’s worse. It’s maybe 4x to 8x our normal tokens-per-second, but only for like 20 to 40 minutes. Today we either overprovision and pay for idle GPUs or we throttle and it blows up downstream.

[01:39] Sara Liu: And we also saw last quarter when we tried to run it on our own vLLM cluster, we ended up in tail-latency hell because someone else was also doing a batch job, and the scheduler… anyway.

[01:52] Markus Klein: Got it. The v1 burst feature is designed exactly for that “short spike, don’t pay forever” scenario, with strict noisy-neighbor protections.

[02:03] Dylan Moore: When you say “burst”, is it basically spot instances? Like you’re going to preempt us if you need the fleet back?

[02:10] Jordan Lee: Good question. Not spot market in v1. It’s more like: you have a dedicated baseline pool reserved for you, and then you can be *admitted* into a separate burst pool that is shared but controlled. The key thing is admission control. If we can’t admit safely, we reject quickly.

[02:27] Mina Haddad: And routing-wise, it’s an explicit step. We try baseline first. If baseline can’t meet the request within the configured SLO constraints and you’re eligible for burst, we try burst. If burst denies, we either fall back to a configured alternative (model variant or region) or we deny back to client.

[02:47] Amit Shah: Okay, so the admission is like, per request?

[02:50] Jordan Lee: Per request, yes. Practically it’s per “routing decision” at the front door. It evaluates: is tenant burst-enabled, is region eligible, are you inside your per-tenant burst limits, and is the pool below saturation gates.

[03:07] Sara Liu: “Saturation gates” meaning what exactly.

[03:10] Jordan Lee: Things like: pool utilization, queued requests, and a safety margin. If we’re beyond threshold, we stop admitting burst for that pool. That’s the circuit breaker idea.

[03:22] Peter Holtz: And we’d rather deny than degrade. You’ll see rejects go up before you see a big p99 blowout. That’s the design.

[03:31] Grace Kim: Shared pool sounds like multi-tenant. Can you confirm isolation? Like, are we running on the same Kubernetes nodes as the hosted API customers.

[03:42] Markus Klein: Great question. The burst pools are separate capacity from the core hosted fleet. They are still shared across *eligible Dedicated tenants*, but with strict guardrails. We can share a written topology doc after this.

[03:56] Grace Kim: So it’s not the public hosted endpoints.

[03:59] Mina Haddad: Correct. Requests still go through your Dedicated tenant ingress; the backend placement can route to baseline dedicated pool or a burst pool, but it remains in the Dedicated control plane context.

[04:12] Logan Wright: And importantly, audit logs and metering stay per tenant. Even if compute is shared, the usage attribution is not.

[04:18] Sara Liu: Can you talk about the per-tenant limits? Like we need to prevent ourselves from accidentally blasting.

[04:25] Jordan Lee: Yeah. The core knobs we have in pilot are:
- max burst concurrency (in-flight requests admitted to burst)
- max burst tokens per second (or token rate budget)
- optional max burst requests per second
- cooldown settings after bursts, so you can’t thrash
- and eligibility constraints like region + GPU class

[04:46] Amit Shah: Can we do time windows? Like only allow Friday 9 to 11.

[04:51] Jordan Lee: We have “burst windows” in the schema draft, yes, but for pilot we’re likely to keep it simple: always-on eligibility with hard caps. Time windows may be there but not the first thing we rely on operationally.

[05:07] Mina Haddad: One thing we want to avoid is a bunch of complicated schedules that become on-call issues. Hard caps are safer.

[05:15] Dylan Moore: How do you set tokens per second? Like we don’t know our exact tokens. It varies by prompt.

[05:22] Logan Wright: We typically estimate from historical usage. We can also do a ramp test. The control plane uses recent moving averages and counters; it’s not perfect per-request but it’s accurate enough to enforce the budget.

[05:35] Sara Liu: So if we exceed the tokens/sec cap, we get denied.

[05:38] Jordan Lee: Yes, you’d get a deny. And we return a reason code in headers so you can tell “tenant cap exceeded” versus “pool saturated” versus “not eligible.”

[05:51] Amit Shah: Let’s talk about those denies. Is it a 429 or 503? Our retry logic depends on that.

[05:58] Mina Haddad: We’re still finalizing, but directionally: if you hit *your configured limit*, that’s a 429-ish semantics. If the pool is saturated or circuit breaker is on, that’s closer to 503. But we also include a stable `x-redwood-burst-deny-reason` header.

[06:19] Peter Holtz: And we’ll provide guidance: 429 = backoff and/or shed; 503 = you can retry with jitter but it might not recover until the pool cools down.

[06:31] Sara Liu: Okay. We’d want to differentiate. Because if it’s “you hit your cap” then retries are pointless.

[06:36] Mina Haddad: Exactly.

[06:38] Dylan Moore: What about preemption? If we’re admitted and then someone else needs capacity, do we get kicked out mid generation.

[06:46] Jordan Lee: In v1 we’re avoiding preemption. So once admitted, it should run to completion. The control is at admission. There are still failure modes (node failure, etc.) but not “we took it away because another tenant showed up.”

[07:02] Amit Shah: That’s reassuring.

[07:04] Sara Liu: But what if the pool is mis-sized and everyone gets in and then it melts.

[07:10] Peter Holtz: That’s where the saturation gates and global circuit breaker come in. We try very hard to not admit into a pool that is on the edge.

[07:20] Mina Haddad: Also we use fairness. If multiple tenants are trying to burst at the same time, we don’t allow one tenant to take the entire pool.

[07:30] Amit Shah: Is fairness like weighted? Like we pay more and we get more.

[07:35] Markus Klein: Commercially there will be tiers. For the design partner pilot, we’ll set explicit per-tenant caps and potentially weights if needed. But we’re not doing an auction or anything fancy.

[07:49] Jordan Lee: The algorithm is basically: hard caps first, then per-tenant share constraints, then pool health.

[08:00] Dylan Moore: I’m going to ask a dumb routing question. If baseline is saturated, why not always go to burst first.

[08:07] Mina Haddad: Not dumb. Baseline is your guaranteed performance and isolation. Going baseline first keeps behavior predictable and keeps burst as an exception. Also burst has its own limits and can be denied.

[08:20] Sara Liu: When does it decide baseline is saturated. Like do you queue, or do you measure.

[08:26] Mina Haddad: We use signals: current queue depth, estimated time-to-first-token, recent p95 service time, plus your configured SLO targets. If baseline would miss, we attempt burst. We avoid long queuing because it kills tails.

[08:45] Amit Shah: So there’s a little bit of prediction.

[08:47] Mina Haddad: Yes, but bounded. It’s not ML magic, it’s heuristics with guardrails.

[08:55] Grace Kim: Residency. If we’re in us-east, does burst ever route to, like, us-west.

[09:03] Jordan Lee: Default is same region. Cross-region would be explicit opt-in, and even then, for pilot we probably won’t enable it unless there’s a strong reason.

[09:14] Grace Kim: Okay, because our data residency is strict.

[09:18] Markus Klein: Understood.

[09:20] Logan Wright: On the monitoring side, you’ll be able to see burst usage per region anyway, so if anything changed you’d see it.

[09:29] Sara Liu: What monitoring do we actually get. Like right now we see request counts and latency, but we need more to operationalize.

[09:37] Logan Wright: For burst we’re planning customer-visible metrics in Console/API:
- burst_admitted_requests
- burst_denied_requests (by reason bucket)
- burst_tokens (shadow metered at first)
- baseline vs burst latency breakdown (TTFT and total)
And we’ll give recommended alerts like “deny rate > X% for Y minutes”.

[10:03] Amit Shah: Will we see pool saturation.

[10:06] Logan Wright: We probably won’t expose raw pool saturation percent because it’s shared and can leak info. But we can expose a “pool availability” indicator or a coarse status.

[10:18] Sara Liu: Hmm. We’d still want to know if it’s us versus you.

[10:22] Peter Holtz: That’s why the deny reason splits are important. “tenant_limit_exceeded” is on you, “pool_saturated” is on us / global condition.

[10:34] Dylan Moore: Can we have different limits by model. We have a smaller model for chat and a bigger one for batch summarize.

[10:42] Jordan Lee: Per-model limits are on the roadmap. For pilot, we can scope eligibility by “routes” and allowlist models for burst, but fine-grained per-model token budgets might come in later.

[10:57] Mina Haddad: But we can support fallback semantics per route: e.g., route A can fall back to a smaller model if burst denies, route B should hard fail.

[11:10] Amit Shah: That’s important. For batch, we can degrade quality, for interactive chat we’d rather fail fast than give weird output.

[11:18] Mina Haddad: Exactly. We’ve been framing it as: choose your failure mode: deny, fallback model, or fallback region (if allowed).

[11:28] Sara Liu: And “fallback” happens after burst deny, not before.

[11:32] Mina Haddad: Typically yes. Baseline → burst attempt → fallback if configured. But we can tune based on route type.

[11:42] Markus Klein: We’ll capture your preferences per endpoint.

[11:46] Grace Kim: Audit logs. If you change the burst limits or enable burst, do we get audit trails.

[11:53] Jordan Lee: Yes. Config changes are audited (who/what/when). Also policy decisions can be logged internally; customer-visible audit events are more limited but the admin actions are visible.

[12:09] Grace Kim: And encryption. If it’s the same region, keys?

[12:12] Markus Klein: Same Dedicated data plane controls. Your traffic is still TLS in transit, and storage follows your tenancy settings. Burst doesn’t change your data retention policy.

[12:25] Dylan Moore: Sorry if I missed: is prompt logging ever on by default.

[12:29] Markus Klein: No, not by default. Same as today.

[12:33] Sara Liu: Let’s get into numbers. Suppose our baseline is 500 requests/minute and spikes to 2,500 for 30 minutes. Concurrency maybe 300. How do we set burst caps.

[12:45] Jordan Lee: We’d set max burst concurrency perhaps to something like 2x baseline concurrency, but we want to align with pool headroom. The burst pool per region is finite. For pilot we’ll size it based on design partner needs plus margin.

[13:02] Peter Holtz: Also we add cooldown. If you burst hard for 30 minutes, we may require a cool-down window to prevent back-to-back saturation events.

[13:11] Amit Shah: Cooldown meaning we can’t burst again.

[13:13] Peter Holtz: Meaning: the admission thresholds get tighter after sustained high usage. It prevents oscillation where everyone keeps spiking and the pool never recovers.

[13:25] Sara Liu: Is cooldown per tenant or global.

[13:28] Jordan Lee: Both exist conceptually. There’s per-tenant backoff and global circuit breaker. The pilot will likely start with a global threshold plus a per-tenant “ramp rate.”

[13:43] Dylan Moore: We can live with that as long as it’s predictable.

[13:47] Mina Haddad: Predictability is why we avoid preemption.

[13:51] Sara Liu: What about request types. We do long context sometimes. Like 32k.

[13:58] Mina Haddad: Long context is more expensive on GPU memory and can distort batching. We may treat those routes differently. For burst pools, we might enforce a max context length or separate pool classes.

[14:12] Amit Shah: So we might not be able to burst long context.

[14:15] Mina Haddad: Not necessarily “not able”, but it would need explicit sizing and we’d likely set lower concurrency for that route.

[14:24] Logan Wright: And we can give you visibility: you’ll see your admitted burst broken down by route category, not necessarily by model in v1.

[14:35] Sara Liu: Are you sampling metrics. We’ve been bitten by missing data.

[14:39] Logan Wright: For high-cardinality dimensions, yes we sample, but core counters like admit/deny are not sampled at the tenant level. Internally we sample some per-model/per-route breakdowns.

[14:53] Amit Shah: Okay.

[14:55] Markus Klein: Maybe we should walk through an end-to-end flow example.

[15:00] Mina Haddad: Sure. Example: HelioPay request comes in to your Dedicated endpoint in us-east. Router looks at baseline pool signals. If baseline is below thresholds, it goes baseline. If baseline is at risk (queue depth high, predicted TTFT over threshold), router calls policy service: “is burst allowed for tenant=HelioPay, region=us-east, route=batch-summarize.” Policy checks your config: burst enabled, allowed in us-east, max burst concurrency not exceeded, token budget okay, global pool health okay. If yes, we route to burst pool. If no, we choose next step: fallback model (if you configured), fallback region (if allowed), else return deny.

[15:42] Sara Liu: And deny comes quickly.

[15:44] Mina Haddad: Yes, we try not to hold it in a queue.

[15:48] Dylan Moore: When you route to burst pool, does it affect baseline. Like do we lose baseline capacity.

[15:54] Jordan Lee: No, baseline is still your reserved pool. Burst is additive capacity, not a trade.

[16:02] Sara Liu: Unless burst causes contention on some shared component, like network.

[16:06] Peter Holtz: We isolate as much as possible. There are shared control plane components, but compute pools are isolated. We’re also setting SLOs around “neighbor p99 drift” specifically to catch any bleed-over.

[16:23] Grace Kim: “Neighbor” meaning other tenants.

[16:25] Peter Holtz: Exactly. We monitor that enabling burst for one tenant doesn’t degrade others beyond a budget.

[16:33] Amit Shah: Can you share those SLOs.

[16:35] Peter Holtz: We can share the high-level ones, yes. Like burst admission success rate target and tail-latency guardrails.

[16:44] Logan Wright: And we’ll likely expose a “burst admission rate” to you, which is basically admitted / attempted, so you can tell if you’re relying on burst and it’s not available.

[16:57] Sara Liu: That’s key. If admission is low during our month-end, we need to know early.

[17:02] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[17:04] Dylan Moore: How do you size the burst pool. Like are we guaranteed some headroom.

[17:10] Markus Klein: In beta, it’s best effort within configured caps and the pool size. In GA, we’re planning a contractable included headroom concept, but in pilot we’ll be explicit: we’ll commit to a certain burst ceiling and communicate availability expectations.

[17:28] Amit Shah: Okay, so it’s not infinite.

[17:30] Markus Klein: Definitely not.

[17:32] Sara Liu: We’re okay with “not infinite” as long as denial is predictable and safe.

[17:37] Mina Haddad: That’s the point of the strict admission approach.

[17:40] Grace Kim: Can other customers burst at the same time and push us out.

[17:45] Jordan Lee: They can reduce availability if the pool is shared, yes. But fairness limits reduce the chance one tenant consumes everything.

[17:55] Peter Holtz: Also we have the ability to disable burst per tenant in an incident, and to adjust weights. But that’s internal ops.

[18:04] Sara Liu: If that happens, how do we know.

[18:07] Logan Wright: You’d see denial reasons shift to “pool_saturated” or “circuit_breaker.” We can also set up a status page event if it’s widespread.

[18:18] Amit Shah: Let’s talk about fallback model. We currently do large model for quality, but can accept smaller for batch. Can you do something like: try baseline large, try burst large, then fallback to small baseline.

[18:33] Mina Haddad: Yes, though the exact chain we support in pilot might be limited to avoid combinatorial complexity. But conceptually: primary model baseline, then burst same model, then fallback to smaller model (could be in baseline or also allowed to burst).

[18:49] Dylan Moore: And you can mark “small model output acceptable.”

[18:52] Mina Haddad: Right. You’d configure per-route policy.

[18:57] Sara Liu: If you fallback to a smaller model, can we know via headers.

[19:01] Mina Haddad: Yes, we already return model version in response metadata, and we can add a “fallback_taken=true” style field if needed.

[19:09] Logan Wright: From metrics side, we track it too.

[19:14] Grace Kim: Does fallback ever change compliance. Like if small model is hosted and big is dedicated.

[19:20] Markus Klein: In your case, both models would be under Dedicated. We wouldn’t fall back to hosted without explicit opt-in. That’s not part of the burst product.

[19:30] Grace Kim: Okay.

[19:32] Sara Liu: We should also talk about rate limiting. We currently use client-side throttles. If burst denies, do you recommend we push back immediately.

[19:41] Peter Holtz: Generally yes. The best practice is: if deny reason is tenant_limit_exceeded, treat it like a hard throttle: do not retry immediately. If it’s pool_saturated, you can retry with exponential backoff and jitter, but you should have a cap.

[19:59] Sara Liu: We can implement that if you give us stable reason codes.

[20:02] Jordan Lee: That’s the plan.

[20:04] Dylan Moore: Sorry, one more. If we’re doing streaming responses, does burst change anything.

[20:10] Mina Haddad: No change. The streaming semantics are the same. The only difference is which backend pool executes the request.

[20:18] Markus Klein: Maybe now we should ask you: what’s your “acceptable degradation”. Like do you prefer denies over slower.

[20:26] Amit Shah: For interactive endpoints, we’d prefer deny over >10 seconds TTFT. For batch, we can accept slower but we have deadlines.

[20:38] Sara Liu: And we want to avoid cascading. A slow response can time out upstream and then we retry and it’s a storm.

[20:47] Peter Holtz: Exactly. That’s why deny fast is healthier.

[20:51] Mina Haddad: For batch, we can consider letting baseline queue a little more before bursting, but we need to be careful.

[21:00] Dylan Moore: Today we’re using a fixed concurrency. We can adjust.

[21:04] Logan Wright: If you send us your trace, we can recommend concurrency and token budget caps.

[21:11] Amit Shah: We’ll do that.

[21:13] Grace Kim: On the security side, we’ll need documentation of isolation. Specifically: are the burst pools in the same VPC, same subnets, etc.

[21:24] Markus Klein: Understood. We have a draft topology doc. I’ll send after the call.

[21:29] Grace Kim: And audit logs for config changes. Preferably exportable.

[21:34] Jordan Lee: We can export admin events. We’ll confirm exact fields.

[21:40] Sara Liu: Are you going to roll this out gradually. We don’t want to be first in production.

[21:45] Markus Klein: This is a private beta. You’d be one of 2 to 3 design partners. We’ll do staged enablement: region by region, and feature-flagged by tenant. We also have a one-command disable.

[22:00] Peter Holtz: And game day drills before we enable in prod.

[22:05] Sara Liu: Love that.

[22:06] Dylan Moore: Can we be part of the game day.

[22:09] Peter Holtz: Yes, we can coordinate.

[22:13] Mina Haddad: We’d run scenarios like: pool saturation, misconfigured tenant caps, routing fallback bug. We validate that deny rates and p99 stay within guardrails.

[22:28] Amit Shah: Cool.

[22:30] Sara Liu: Let’s revisit observability. Would we get dashboards or just raw metrics.

[22:35] Logan Wright: Both. In Console we’ll have a dashboard with “baseline vs burst” and deny reasons over time. We can also expose Prometheus-style export (depending on your integration) or via API.

[22:49] Sara Liu: We use Datadog.

[22:51] Logan Wright: We can integrate via our metrics export. We’ll share the naming. Internally we use Grafana.

[22:58] Dylan Moore: Billing. Are we going to see line items.

[23:01] Markus Klein: In pilot, it’s shadow metered. Meaning we attribute usage as baseline vs burst but we may not invoice immediately while we validate. We will share the report so you can sanity check.

[23:16] Amit Shah: Okay, that’s fine.

[23:18] Sara Liu: One question: what happens if baseline is fine but we still want to use burst, like to finish faster.

[23:24] Mina Haddad: Today it’s not a “force burst” flag; it’s policy-driven. We can discuss adding a “prefer_burst” route policy later, but it complicates fairness.

[23:36] Jordan Lee: And it can create a tragedy-of-commons. Everyone wants burst even when baseline is okay.

[23:41] Sara Liu: Makes sense.

[23:44] Dylan Moore: How do you prevent a single tenant from sending like a million tiny requests and hogging.

[23:50] Jordan Lee: That’s why we have both concurrency and token-rate controls. If you send tiny requests, concurrency/rps caps catch it. If you send big tokens, token budget catches it.

[24:04] Peter Holtz: Also global pool protection: if the pool’s health degrades, we close admission.

[24:11] Sara Liu: We’ll need to know if our clients should reduce request size, like smaller max_tokens.

[24:17] Mina Haddad: That’s a good lever. We can recommend dynamic max_tokens under deny pressure.

[24:23] Amit Shah: We can implement that.

[24:26] Markus Klein: Can I ask about your endpoints. Are these all chat completions, or you also do embeddings.

[24:33] Dylan Moore: Mostly chat/generation. Some embeddings but those are separate.

[24:38] Mina Haddad: Embeddings could burst too, but we may treat it separately because it’s throughput oriented.

[24:46] Sara Liu: Another operational thing: if you deny, are you returning quickly enough that our load balancer doesn’t consider it a “slow” error.

[24:54] Mina Haddad: Yes, deny is basically immediate. A few milliseconds to tens.

[25:00] Sara Liu: Great.

[25:02] Grace Kim: What about data retention on logs for burst. Is anything extra logged.

[25:07] Logan Wright: We log decision metadata: admitted/denied, reason code, pool label, but not your prompt content. Retention follows standard Dedicated logs.

[25:19] Grace Kim: Okay.

[25:21] Sara Liu: Alright. I think the key is: reason codes, stable response codes, and us-east-only.

[25:28] Markus Klein: That matches what we heard.

[25:31] Mina Haddad: We should also confirm your desired fallback behavior. For batch: allow fallback to smaller model. For interactive: deny if baseline+burst fails.

[25:42] Amit Shah: Yes.

[25:43] Dylan Moore: Also for interactive, we’d rather a 503 than a 429, because then our clients show “service unavailable” not “rate limited.” But I get the semantics.

[25:54] Jordan Lee: We can align on status codes and still keep reason header. We’re iterating.

[26:01] Peter Holtz: The important part is your retry/backoff uses the header not just the status.

[26:06] Sara Liu: Yes.

[26:07] Markus Klein: We’re at about halfway. Any other deep technical concerns.

[26:12] Dylan Moore: I’m curious how you measure tokens per second in real time. Like do you count output tokens only.

[26:18] Logan Wright: Both input and output. We have counters from the serving runtime. There can be slight delays, but it’s sufficient for budgeting.

[26:29] Dylan Moore: Okay.

[26:31] Sara Liu: One more thing: when requests retry, sometimes they reuse the same trace context. Does your policy handle that.

[26:39] Jordan Lee: We’ve seen issues in other systems. Our policy is deterministic per request and uses request IDs; retries are evaluated fresh. We’re careful not to “carry over” an admit.

[26:50] Mina Haddad: And we propagate the admit decision in headers for observability, but we don’t trust it for auth. The server decides.

[27:00] Grace Kim: Good.

[27:02] Amit Shah: Okay, next steps. We’ll send you traffic traces. You send us schema and topology. And then schedule load test.

[27:12] Markus Klein: Yep.

[27:14] Sara Liu: Can you include recommended alert thresholds. Like deny rate >5% for 10 minutes.

[27:20] Logan Wright: Yes, I’ll send a starter pack.

[27:23] Peter Holtz: And we’ll include runbook guidance: what to do if deny spikes (reduce max_tokens, reduce concurrency, or temporarily disable burst).

[27:32] Sara Liu: We’d want the disable option exposed to us or only Redwood.

[27:36] Markus Klein: In pilot, Redwood will do it, but we can discuss customer self-serve in GA. We don’t want accidental toggles.

[27:46] Grace Kim: That’s fine.

[27:48] (crosstalk)

[27:50] Markus Klein: Alright, we’ll follow up via email today. Anything else.

[27:56] Dylan Moore: Not from me.

[27:58] Sara Liu: Good.

[28:00] Grace Kim: Please include the residency statement explicitly.
